languages. Multilingual individuals often exhibit language-specific differences
in their cognitive abilities, which can be leveraged to develop more
effective and adaptive human-computer interfaces. In this paper, we explore
the relationship between the language proficiency of multilingual individuals
and their cognitive abilities. We collected behavioral data from 100
multilingual individuals performing a visual search task in two languages. We
found that the visual search performance of multilingual individuals is
language-dependent. Multilingual individuals perform better in the language
they are more proficient in. We also found that the visual search performance
of multilingual individuals is consistent across different visual stimuli.
Our results can be leveraged to develop adaptive visual search interfaces for
multilingual individuals. For example, visual search interfaces can be
designed to utilize the visual search capabilities of multilingual individuals
more effectively by presenting them with visual stimuli in their native
language.
  We also collected electroencephalography (EEG) data from 20 multilingual
individuals performing the visual search task in two languages. We found that
the language proficiency of multilingual individuals is reflected in the
neural activity of their brain. The neural activity of multilingual individuals
is more efficient in the language they are more proficient in. Our results can
be leveraged to develop adaptive visual search interfaces for multilingual
individuals by presenting them with visual stimuli in a way that minimizes the
neural effort required to search for the stimuli.

known to be suboptimal. In this work, we investigate the impact of using
high-quality, professionally written descriptions from Wikipedia on training
automatic image description systems. We find that using these descriptions
leads to significant improvements in quality. The best model we train achieves
a 12% absolute improvement over the strong baseline model trained on

the quality of the descriptions is not the only factor that matters, but also
the diversity of the set of descriptions. Our analysis shows that the
techniques we employ are effective because they reduce the need for the model to
generalize over a large set of descriptions. Finally, we find that the
improvements we achieve are not limited to the specific task of automatic
image description, but also generalize to other tasks that require

The quality of the speech signal is affected by the acoustic environment in
which the speech is produced. The acoustic environment can be characterized by
the reverberation time, noise level, and background noise type. The acoustic
environment can degrade the quality of the speech signal and also affect the
accuracy of automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems. In this paper, we
propose a novel framework for generating a wide range of acoustic environments
and also train ASR models in such environments. We use the Convolutional
Reverb Generator (CRG) to generate the reverberation time from 0.2s to 0.6s
with a step size of 0.1s. We also use the Mozilla Common Voice dataset to train
ASR models using the Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) loss function
and also the Graph Neural Network (GNN) loss function. We use the Switched
Merlin ASR system to train and evaluate our models. We evaluate our models
using the Word Error Rate (WER) metric and also the Character Error Rate (CER)
metric. We achieve a significant improvement in WER and CER when the model is
trained in the reverberant environment compared to the non-reverberant
environment.

entangled photons between distant locations. In this work, we report on the
design, construction, and operation of a 1-km long, free-space quantum
communication link between two buildings on the University of Oxford campus in
the UK. The link uses a 589-nm laser source to generate 1-kW of stable, and
reliable, uplink transmission to a 2-GHz bandwidth, 1550-nm, single-photon
detection system in the receive building. We demonstrate the successful
transmission of 830-nm (V) and 1550-nm (W) entangled photon pairs, generated
using spontaneous parametric down-conversion, over the free-space link with a
total distance of 1.5 km (830 nm + 670 nm). The 830-nm (V) photons are
transmitted through air and detected using a superconducting single-photon
detector, while the 1550-nm (W) photons are transmitted through air and
detected using a shot-noise limited avalanche photodiode. We measure a
correlation visibility of 2.61 $\pm$ 0.07, and a Bell inequality violation of
2.50 $\pm$ 0.09, which clearly demonstrates the violation of local realism.

communication link in a real-world setting and paves the way for the
development of global-scale quantum networks.

10 km, and has been optimized to achieve high key rates and long secure
distances. We have successfully demonstrated the operation of the QKD system

work. The system has achieved a secure key rate of 1.1 kbps and a secure

1951 thesis by T.A. Springer. In this thesis Springer studied the
classification of conjugacy classes in the symplectic group Sp 2n. This study
led to important insights in the structure of symplectic groups and their
representations. The thesis started with a discussion of the symplectic group
defined over a polynomial ring. Springer determined the conjugacy classes in
this group and studied the quotient space. She showed that this quotient
corresponds to the flag variety of the group. The results were used to study
the orthogonal group, starting with the rank one case. The thesis ended with
an important result on the conjugacy classes in the group Sp 2n, which was
later generalized by C.S. Shapiro and N.J. Fineberg. The thesis was
successfully defended by Springer on 18 May 1951.
  The original thesis is not available anymore. Van der Kallen filled in gaps
and added explanations to make the thesis readable again.

Netherlands and the USA. She is best known for her work on the structure of
symplectic and general linear groups and their flag varieties. Her work on the
symplectic group led to important insights in the structure of
representations of the symplectic group. Her work on flag varieties showed that
these varieties are isomorphic to the quotient space of the group by its
maximal torus. This result is now a standard tool in the study of Lie groups
and their representations.

mother. Her husband, David Springer, was a mathematician too. He worked at the
University of Michigan. Her children, Jan and Els, are both married and have
children of their own.

students and postdocs. Her students and collaborators remember her as a
generous and kind person.

understand how different learning algorithms affect the social and individual
outcomes that emerge from competition. We study a simple stochastic game where
two agents learn to play a coordination game. We show that if the agents use
different learning algorithms, the resulting outcomes can be drastically
different. For example, if one agent uses a best-response algorithm and the

while the second will achieve at least half of the optimal payoff. On the other
hand, if both agents use the same learning algorithm, the resulting outcomes
will be identical. We also show that if the agents use different learning
algorithms and the payoffs are not identical, then the limit-average payoff
achieved by one agent can be arbitrarily close to the optimal payoff, while the
other agent achieves a payoff that is arbitrarily far from optimal.

agents in the outcomes that emerge from competition. We also show that even
with simple games and algorithms, the resulting outcomes can be complex and
surprising.

La$_2$Zr$_2$O$_7$ oxide are studied using the combination of the cluster

model used in the cluster simulations, but including the effects of
long-range electronic interactions. We find that the superconducting gap

the experimental value of 0.35K. The results are compared with the
single-band s-wave model, and we show that the La$_2$Zr$_2$O$_7$ superconducting

anisotropic $s+g$ gap.

the La$_2$Zr$_2$O$_7$ model. We find that the cDMFT+AC approach yields
consistent results with the standard cDMFT simulations, and we show that the
AC solver does not change the qualitative features of the La$_2$Zr$_2$O$_7$
electronic structure and superconducting gap function.

electronic structure and superconducting gap function. We find that the removal
of one f-electron is equivalent to the substitution of Zr$^{4+}$ by Zr$^{3+}$,

this work, we theoretically investigate the dynamics of Bose-Einstein condensates
(BECs) in optical lattices with nearest-neighbor interactions. We show that,
depending on the strength of the inter-site interactions, the BEC can exhibit
both quasi-contiguous molecular states and quasi-lattice molecular states. We
furthermore show that the quasi-contiguous molecular states can be dynamically
generated by applying a periodic modulation of the lattice depth. Finally, we

imaging the BEC after a period of time evolution.
  From a theoretical point of view, the description of BECs in optical lattices
is based on the Gross-Pitaevskii equation (GPE). However, the GPE is not
suitable for describing quasi-contiguous molecular states, since it is based on
a local approximation of the interatomic interactions. In order to overcome this
limitation, we have developed a new theoretical approach based on the
tight-binding approximation of the multi-body interactions. This approach
allows us to study the quasi-contiguous molecular states in a full quantum
lattice regime, where the BEC is described by a lattice of quasi-molecules.
Within this approach, we have investigated the ground state and dynamical
properties of BECs in one-dimensional lattices with nearest-neighbor interactions
and we have shown that the quasi-contiguous molecular states can be generated by
applying a periodic modulation of the lattice depth.

the final chapter of this thesis. We show that the quasi-contiguous molecular
states are a general phenomenon that can be observed in both weak- and
strong-interaction regimes. However, the quasi-contiguous molecular states
observed in the weak-interaction regime are more robust against temperature
fluctuations. Finally, we show that the quasi-contiguous molecular states can
be experimentally detected by imaging the BEC after a period of time evolution.

optical lattices, as well as to other systems of interacting particles, such as

provide a unique window into the world of high-energy physics. Due to its large
mass, the top quark decays before hadronization and its decay products are
sensitive to Beyond Standard Model (BSM) effects. The large center-of-mass energy
available at the LHC allows for the study of top quark production in association
with other particles, which are of great interest for precision measurements

quark production in association with top-antitop quark pairs, single vector
bosons and the Higgs boson using proton-proton collision data collected by the
ATLAS experiment at the LHC.

measurements of the top quark mass and properties. Single top quark production
provides sensitivity to the CKM matrix elements and to BSM physics. Top quark
production in association with vector bosons is sensitive to BSM physics and
provides a means to study the electroweak interaction. Top quark production in

implementation shows that the algorithm can efficiently solve the problem for
degree sequences with up to 20 vertices.

prediction of unordered events. We show that our framework is able to leverage
high-quality event representations to predict ordered sequences of unordered
events and outperforms a strong baseline model that leverages event
representations.

events, we also release a new dataset of unordered events, called the
EventOrdering Dataset (EOD). The EOD contains 1,000 events from 10 domains and
is designed to study the task of sequential prediction of unordered events.
With the EOD, researchers can study the task of sequential prediction of
unordered events and develop new models that can be evaluated on the EOD.

Hodge-theory of representation spaces of compact Lie groups in the real vector
bundle $E(G,K)_{\lambda}$, where $G$ is a compact Lie group, $K$ is a closed
subgroup, and $\lambda$ is a highest weight. We show that the Euler-characteristic
of $E(G,K)_{\lambda}$ is the index of the Dirac-operator of the principal
bundle $G \to G/K$. We prove that the Betti-numbers of $E(G,K)_{\lambda}$ are
given by the ranks of the compactly supported cohomology groups of the
quotient-manifold $G/K$ with coefficients in the Verma-module $H(G,K)_{\lambda}$
twisted by a line bundle of degree $\lambda$. In the case where $K=\{e\}$ is
the trivial subgroup, we show that the Betti-numbers of $E(G,K)_{\lambda}$ are
given by the ranks of the compactly supported cohomology groups of $G$ with
coefficients in the Verma-module $H(G,K)_{\lambda}$. Finally, we determine the
Betti-numbers of $E(SU(2),SO(2))_{\lambda}$ for all highest weights $\lambda$.
These results are based on the fact that the cohomology of $E(G,K)_{\lambda}$
is isomorphic to the relative cohomology of the projection $G \to G/K$ with
coefficients in the Verma-module $H(G,K)_{\lambda}$.

in strong-field, pulsed
electromagnetic radiation using a mixture of Rb$^+$ and D$^+$ ions in a
linear Paul trap. The pair creation process is modeled by the relative energy
transfer between the two ions, which is determined by the difference in the
interaction time in the electric field of the pulse. Due to the large mass
difference, the interaction time difference is sensitive to the relative
velocity of the ions, which is controlled by the laser cooling process. The
mass difference also results in a large difference in the ion motion under the
electric field of the pulse, which can be used to enhance the sensitivity of
the energy transfer to the relative velocity. We show that the D$^+$ ion
motion can be used to enhance the signal and reduce the statistical noise.
Using numerical simulations, we show that the proposed method can be used to
detect pair creation probabilities of $10^{-6}$ in a few minutes with a
confidence level of 99\%. We also show that the proposed method can be used
to measure pair creation probabilities as a function of time in the pulse.
Using a 1 kW laser, we estimate that the required peak field strength for
pair creation is $0.15 E_{\rm C}\sim 10^{20} \rm{V/m}$, where $E_{\rm C}$ is
the critical electric field.

  Security screening is a critical process to ensure public safety. X-ray
images are widely used for security screening, and deep learning-based methods
have achieved remarkable success in detecting prohibited items. However,
practical security screening systems are still limited by the high false
positive rate of current methods. In this paper, we propose a novel framework
to reduce the false positive rate of prohibited items detection. Specifically,
we first train a general model to detect general items, and then we fine-tune
the general model to detect specific items. To effectively utilize the general
model, we propose to use the intermediate representations of the general model
to generate pseudo-labels for the unlabeled images, and then we use the
pseudo-labels to train a contrastive learning-based unsupervised distillation
network. Extensive experiments show that our framework achieves superior
results compared to state-of-the-art methods that are trained from scratch
using the labeled data only.

luminosity of 174 inverse nanobarns. The significance of the tt-bar signal

has been recognized as a
promising enabler for the 6G wireless communication systems. The IRS is
capable of reflecting the incident signal in a phase-shift manner to improve
the communication performance. In this paper, we investigate the joint beamforming
and intelligent reflecting surface optimization problem for a multi-user multiple-input
multiple-output (MIMO) system. The objective is to maximize the total weighted
sum-rate of the multi-user MIMO system with the assistance of the IRS. To
solve the non-convex optimization problem, we propose an alternating optimization
algorithm. In each iteration of the proposed algorithm, we first fix the
reflecting coefficients of the IRS and update the beamformers of all the
single-antenna users via a convex-concave procedure (CCP) based algorithm. Then,
we fix the beamformers of all the single-antenna users and update the reflecting
coefficients of the IRS via a convex optimization problem. The simulation results
show that the proposed alternating optimization algorithm achieves a sum-rate
performance close to the joint optimization benchmark. Moreover, the proposed
algorithm outperforms the existing multi-agent optimization algorithm in terms
of sum-rate performance and convergence speed.

scans of a deformable rubber duck. Our results show that our approach is able

over finite fields. We show that this construction can be used to give new
solutions to several systems of polynomial equations over the integers. These
systems correspond to classical problems in number theory, including the
solution to certain quartic Thue equations and the computation of certain
modular forms. We also show that the solutions obtained from the construction
satisfy specific symmetry conditions, which reflects the structure of the
designs and the choice of parameters in the construction.

degree four and derive the complete solution over the integers. The solution
involves the use of modular forms and the fact that the Thue equation can be
transformed into a system of four quadratic forms. We also show that the
construction of Amarra, Devillers and Praeger can be used to give solutions to
certain systems of polynomial equations over finite fields which correspond to
the computation of modular forms. This shows that the construction is
connected to number theoretic problems, but the specific parameters and
structure of the design is needed to derive solutions over the integers.
  Finally, we show that the solutions to the Thue equation and the systems of
equations considered in the first part of the paper can be encoded into
specific binary sequences. These sequences have specific properties which
reflect the structure of the solutions and the use of modular forms in their
derivation.

constraints on the parameter space of the BSM from the dark matter relic

experiments.

broken by one or more scalar fields. We show that in this case the dark
matter is a mixture of the $B-L$ gauge boson and the scalar(s). We present
constraints on the parameter space of this model from the dark matter relic
density, direct detection, and collider searches. We show that this model
predicts a rich phenomenology, and that it can be tested in several
experiments.

broken and the dark matter is a scalar particle. We present constraints on
the parameter space of this model from the dark matter relic density, direct
detection, and collider searches. We show that this model predicts a rich
phenomenology, and that it can be tested in several experiments.

broken and the dark matter is a fermion. We present constraints on the
parameter space of this model from the dark matter relic density, direct

lattice) leads to an effective mass for the Dirac electrons. The mass is
proportional to the number of vacancies and can be controlled experimentally.
We also show that vacancies induce long-range Coulomb interactions between
electrons. We model these effects using a tight-binding Hamiltonian and
perform a renormalization group analysis to study the low-energy behavior of
electrons in the presence of vacancies. We find that vacancies lead to an
effective mass, but do not change the universality class of the electron-electron
interactions. We also find that the mass and interactions compete in the
determination of the ground state. We show that the competition between the
effective mass and interactions can be tuned by changing the doping level in
graphene. Our results can be used to study the behavior of electrons in
graphene and other Dirac materials in the presence of vacancies.
  From a theoretical point of view, the presence of vacancies in graphene
introduces a tunable parameter that can be used to study the behavior of Dirac
fermions in the presence of an effective mass. This is an interesting
theoretical problem that can be addressed using renormalization group methods.
However, in order to apply these methods, we need to model the effects of
vacancies in graphene. In this work, we show that vacancies can be modeled by
removing atoms from the lattice. This is a simple and intuitive approach that
can be used to study the effects of vacancies in graphene.
  We also show that vacancies lead to long-range Coulomb interactions between
electrons. This is an important effect that can be used to study the behavior
of electrons in graphene in the presence of vacancies. In particular, we show
that vacancies can be used to tune the interactions between electrons in
graphene. This is an important result that can be used to study the behavior of
electrons in graphene in the presence of vacancies.

lattice. This leads to an effective mass for Dirac electrons and long-range
Coulomb interactions. The mass and interactions compete in the determination
of the ground state and can be tuned by changing the doping level in graphene.
This is an interesting theoretical problem that can be addressed using
renormalization group methods.

consistent with the expected age of the Kepler-452b planetary system, which

  In the last years, the study of the properties of mesons has become a
fundamental task in the study of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD). The study of
mesons is of great importance because they are the lightest bound states of

strongly interacting matter. In addition, mesons are the building blocks of

full theory. In this work we will focus on two of the most popular effective
theories for mesons: the non-relativistic QCD (NRQCD) and the relativistic
quark-diquark effective theory (RQD).

neutrons stars (NSs). In this work, we explore the impact of the EOS on the
merger dynamics of binary neutron star (BNS) systems. We perform a set of
simulations using the same numerical code but with different EOSs, namely the
Togashi et al. (2015) (TG) and Harte et al. (2019) (H4) EOSs, which are
compatible with the 1.4 $M_\odot$ mass constraint and are representative of the
range of possible EOSs. We find that the merger dynamics is sensitive to the
EOS, with the H4 EOS leading to a more compact NS at coalescence, and a more
dynamical and eccentric inspiral. The H4 EOS also results in a more massive
remnant, with a larger baryonic mass, and a more massive and massive disk. We
also find that the H4 EOS leads to a more robust and long-lived post-merger
signal, with a longer duration of the signal, and a more pronounced $g$-mode
oscillation. We find that the H4 EOS can explain the GW170817 event without the
need of a substantial amount of ejecta. We also find that the H4 EOS can
produce a robust and long-lived signal that can be detected by the third
generation of ground-based detectors for a large fraction of the BNS merger
population.
  We also investigate the impact of the choice of the EOS on the nucleation of
a hypermassive NS (HMNS) and the formation of a supramassive NS (SMNS). We
find that the HMNS nucleation is more likely to occur with the H4 EOS, while
the SMNS formation is more likely to occur with the TG EOS.
  Finally, we find that the H4 EOS can be constrained by the detection of a
single BNS event, while the TG EOS is consistent with the current data. We
conclude that the choice of the EOS is crucial for the BNS merger simulations
and that future observations can help to constrain the EOS of matter at
supranuclear densities.

Earth is that the diversity of life has increased over time. This diversity
increase is often cited as evidence for the gradualism of evolution, but it is
also a challenge to the neutral theory of molecular evolution, which
predicts that diversity should be constant over time. Here, we show that the
diversity increase can be explained by the neutral theory, and that the
diversity increase is an artifact of the way diversity is measured. We show
that the neutral theory can explain the tempo of originations and extinctions
of animal body plans on Earth, and that the rate of speciation is roughly
equal to the rate of extinction. We also show that the diversity increase is
confounded by the fact that animals are much more diverse than other animals
(specifically, metazoans are much more diverse than sponges). Finally, we show
that the neutral theory can explain the tempo of originations and extinctions
of other animal body plans, including those of cnidarians, bilaterians, and
deuterostomes.

Broadbent and Lord (TQC'20), is an
encryption scheme that guarantees that any attempt to copy ciphertexts will
result in unclonable forgeries. Broadbent and Lord showed that such a scheme is
possible based on quantum hardness of learning with errors (LWE) assumption.
In this paper, we show that similar results can be achieved under quantum
hardness of ring-LWE (RLWE) assumption. Our construction is also inspired by
Broadbent and Lord's construction, and the main tool is a hash-and-sign paradigm
using a variant of Brakerski-Figuereda's reencryption scheme from
(quantum) RLWE assumption. We show that if the reencryption keys are
authenticated with a message authentication code (MAC) secure against
quantum polynomial-time adversaries, then the resulting encryption scheme
satisfies unclonability against quantum polynomial-time adversaries.
  We also show that the unclonable encryption scheme can be instantiated with
very efficient reencryption schemes, resulting in a very efficient
unclonable encryption scheme. Our construction is also generic, in the sense
that it can be instantiated with various reencryption schemes, and the choice
of reencryption scheme can be based on the desired trade-off between
reencryption and unclonability capabilities of the resulting unclonable
encryption scheme.

introduce the necessary background and definitions. In Section~\ref{sec:our
construction}, we present our construction of unclonable encryption from
(quantum) RLWE assumption. In Section~\ref{sec:security}, we show the security
of our construction. In Section~\ref{sec:instantiations}, we show that our
construction can be instantiated with very efficient reencryption schemes.
Finally, in Section~\ref{sec:discussion}, we discuss our construction and its
trade-offs.

graphene. The presence of SOPE is evidenced by the observation of spin-orbit

sequential data. These models are often used in natural language processing
(NLP) for tasks such as language modeling and machine translation. In NLP,
neural models are typically trained and evaluated on large datasets. However,
these models are often deployed in settings where data is limited, such as in
low-resource language translation. In this paper, we investigate the
performance of sequential neural networks models when trained on small
datasets. We find that sequential neural networks models trained on small
datasets retain a significant amount of information about the training data,
and that this information interferes with their ability to generalize. We
propose a simple method for debiasing these models, and find that it is
effective in improving their ability to generalize. We also find that the
performance of debiased models is highly dependent on the choice of training
data, and that there is a tradeoff between the size of the training data and
the quality of the training data.

neutrino oscillation experiments require accurate knowledge of the neutrino

for neutrino energy reconstruction in long-baseline neutrino oscillation

variations in training conditions and was able to generalize to real data.

anisotropic order parameter is still not well understood. In particular, the
behavior of such a superconductor in the presence of a magnetic field is
complex and depends on the orientation of the order parameter with respect to

linearized Ginzburg-Landau equations in a rotating reference frame. This

orientation of the magnetic vortex is determined by the orientation of the
order parameter with respect to the rotating magnetic field. The magnetic
vortex is a stable feature of the magnetization of the superconductor, and it
may be used to explain the complex magnetization curves observed in

investigate the ground state of the heavy fermion compound YbAgGe. In the
magnetic field range from 0 to 65 T, we find that the ground state changes from
an antiferromagnet to a field-induced superconductor. The superconducting
transition temperature increases with magnetic field in a way that is
consistent with a Pauli limited orbital limited superconductor. The
superconducting state is also characterized by a large critical field, and by
a strong suppression of the attenuation in zero bias, consistent with
superconductivity in YbAgGe being driven by magnetic field induced pairing of
the heavy quasiparticles.
  The superconducting state of YbAgGe is also characterized by a large
resistivity anomaly at low temperatures and high magnetic fields, which we
interpret as a field-induced magnetic transition at the N\'eel temperature of
the antiferromagnet. This anomaly is suppressed in magnetic fields above the
superconducting critical field, consistent with the antiferromagnetic order
being suppressed by the magnetic field in a way that is consistent with a
magnetic exchange interaction between the Yb$^{3+}$ ions and the conduction
electrons.

between the Yb$^{3+}$ ions and the conduction electrons.

compared to other heavy fermion compounds.

MIMO systems in a
scattering environment. We consider a multi-user multiple access channel with
single-antenna users and a base station equipped with a large number of multi-
element arrays. We assume that the channel is time-varying and scattering is
present between the users and the base station. We derive the asymptotic
performance of the maximum-ratio combining (MRC) receiver in terms of the
asymptotic signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), the asymptotic rate, and the asymptotic
error probability. We show that the asymptotic performance depends on the
scattering properties, the array geometry, and the number of antennas. We
derive conditions for the asymptotic rate to be increased by increasing the
number of antennas. We also derive conditions for the error probability to be
decreased by increasing the number of antennas. We show that the asymptotic
performance can be improved by optimizing the array geometry. We also show how
the asymptotic performance can be improved by using the scattering between the
users and the base station.
  We show that the results can be used to design optimal arrays for MRC. We
propose a new optimization problem that takes into account the scattering
between the users and the base station. We show that the optimal array geometry
is the one that minimizes the scattering between the users and the base station.
We also show that the optimal array geometry can be obtained by solving a
convex optimization problem. We propose a heuristic algorithm that can be used
to obtain the optimal array geometry. We show that the proposed algorithm can
be used to obtain arrays with improved performance. We also show that the
proposed algorithm can be used to obtain arrays with reduced number of
antennas.

possible for every pair of vertices x and y of G. Equitable total chromatic
number of a graph G denoted by x_et(G) is the minimum number of colors required

as zero-energy modes at superconductors with non-Abelian topological order or

challenging, as it requires the measurement of zero-energy peaks in the
spectroscopic response of a nanoscale device. Here, we show that Majorana
zero-energy modes at a magnetic topological insulator (MTI) should be
characterized by a non-zero dc Josephson current in a superconducting MTI

topological phase of the MTI that can convert a spin current into a charge
current. We demonstrate this phenomenon in a device consisting of a superconducting
lead deposited on top of a magnetic topological insulator, where we observe a
persistent dc current with a magnitude of 1.5 nA and a direction that is
reversible upon reversal of the magnetic field. Our results provide a direct
signature of the non-Abelian topological phase of the MTI and open the way to
detect Majorana fermions in such systems.

is a widely used technique for
improving the dynamic range of images. However, it is often limited by the
availability of multiple exposures. In this paper, we propose a novel approach
to HDR imaging that uses a single exposure and a learned prior. We train a
generative adversarial network (GAN) to synthesize HDR images from low dynamic
range ones. The network consists of two stages: a progressive upsampling stage
and a detail injection stage. The progressive upsampling stage gradually adds
more details to the HDR image by increasing the spatial resolution of the
feature maps. The detail injection stage adds high-frequency details to the
output of the progressive upsampling stage. We train the network using a
perceptual loss function that combines a adversarial loss with a HDR loss.
Experimental results show that our method can produce HDR images with a
dynamic range similar to that of state-of-the-art multi-exposure HDR methods.
Moreover, our method can produce HDR images from low dynamic range images with
a lower peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) error compared to state-of-the-art
single-exposure HDR methods.

is a rapidly growing field of research that aims
to improve the reliability of machine learning (ML) models by incorporating
domain knowledge about causality. However, CDL is still in its infancy, and
there is a lack of systematic evaluation of existing methods. In this work, we
propose a framework for evaluating causal ML models based on the causal graph
structure of the data. We define a new metric called causal performance (CP)
that measures the degree to which a model captures the causal relationships in
the data. We then use CP to evaluate a range of causal and non-causal ML
models on a variety of datasets. Our results show that CP is able to
systematically distinguish between causal and non-causal models, and that it
can be used to identify the best model for a given task. We also find that
existing CDL methods are not as effective at capturing causal relationships as
we would expect, and we propose a number of improvements to existing methods
that can be made to increase their causal performance. Finally, we use CP to
evaluate a CDL pipeline that incorporates domain knowledge about causality and
shows how CP can be used to evaluate the performance of the resulting models.
We hope that our work will help to facilitate further research into CDL, and
will provide a framework for evaluating the performance of causal ML models.

fundamental for the efficiency of chemical processes. In this work, we present a
novel inverse problem formulation to control the temperature distribution inside
a catalytic reactor. The goal is to steer the temperature to a desired
distribution. To this end, we consider a feedback linearization technique
combined with a gain-scheduling controller. The feedback linearization
technique is used to cancel the heat transfer term in the partial differential
equation (PDE) model of the temperature field, which is then replaced by a
set of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) describing the temperature of
the catalytic particles. The gain-scheduling controller is then used to
steer the ODEs to the desired temperature distribution. The gain scheduling
activation temperature is determined by a least squares minimization problem
solved off-line. The performance of the proposed controller is illustrated in
a numerical example and compared with a classical finite element method
solution.

temperature distribution to the desired distribution with a lower computational
cost compared to the finite element method solution.

element method solution.

average accuracy of 0.64 and mean squared error of 0.19.

important than audio features for attention estimation. We also find that
recurrent networks are more effective than convolutional networks for
attention estimation.

estimation in advertising. We find that attention estimation can help in

an overview of the relationship between
Hodge-theoretic and geometric compactifications of moduli spaces of algebraic
varieties. We focus on the case of smooth hypersurfaces in P^2.
  Let M_d be the moduli space of smooth degree d hypersurfaces in P^2. Its
Hodge-theoretic compactification, \bar{M}_d, is the Deligne-Mumford compactification
of its Kähler moduli. Geometrically, M_d is the quotient of the space of smooth
triangulations of a degree d nodal curve in P^2 by the group of automorphisms
induced by the automorphisms of the projective plane. The geometric compactification
of moduli of smooth triangulations is the space of stable triangulations,
\mathcal{ST}_d, which is the quotient of the space of stable curves of genus 0 by
the group of automorphisms induced by the automorphisms of the projective line.
We review the results of Arnold and others which show that there is a
correspondence between the Hodge-theoretic and geometric compactifications. This
correspondence is not an isomorphism of varieties, but rather a birational map
which is induced by the Gross-Siebert formula for \bar{M}_d and by the
construction of \mathcal{ST}_d by Keel and Posen.
  We also review the results of the second author which show that the
Hodge-theoretic and geometric compactifications are each cut out by equations
involving the canonical ring of the moduli space and the space of stable
triangulations. These results generalize the classical result of which gives the
equations for the space of smooth curves of genus 0.
  Finally, we review the results of the first author which show that the
Hodge-theoretic and geometric compactifications are each cut out by equations
involving the Milnor invariant of the moduli space and the space of stable
triangulations. These results generalize the classical result of which gives the
equations for the space of smooth curves of genus 0.
  The results of the first and second authors are part of the program of
classifying moduli spaces of algebraic varieties using invariants of
non-commutative geometry. The results of the third author are part of the
program of studying the geometry of the space of stable triangulations.

predicted by a semi-analytic model of galaxy formation that includes a

characterize the functions $f:\left[0,1\right]\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ for which

converges almost surely, where $\gamma_{A,B^{H}}$ is the local time of
$A+B^{H}$ at the point $A$. The result is obtained by means of the study of
the asymptotic behavior of the moments of the integral. The case in which $f$

equivalent to the convergence of the local time at a fixed point. We also
characterize the continuous functions $f:\left[0,1\right]\rightarrow
\mathbb{R}$ for which the process \[ \left\{ \gamma_{A,B^{H}}\left(t\right),

equivalent to the existence of a continuous modification of the local time of

In this work, we focus on the problem of recognizing actions performed by a
single agent in a multi-agent scene. We propose a novel end-to-end framework
that takes audio-visual data as input and outputs the identity of the agent
performing the action. Our framework is composed of a multi-agent action
recognition network (MAAMNet) that is trained using a novel multi-task
learning strategy. The MAAMNet is trained to simultaneously perform two
supervised tasks: action recognition and identity classification. We evaluate
our approach on a multi-agent version of the UCF-101 dataset and a multi-agent
version of the Kinetics-400 dataset. Our results show that the proposed
framework outperforms a single-agent action recognition network by 10% and 5%
on UCF-101 and Kinetics-400, respectively.

with the property that the automorphism group has two orbits on vertices and is

locally arc transitive graphs remains a central theme in the study of vertex
transitive graphs and their automorphism groups. The locally arc transitive
graphs with two orbits on vertices are of particular interest as they provide
examples of quasiprimitive groups of degree infinity, with exactly one orbit on
vertices, of twisted wreath type.
  We also show that the automorphism group of each of these graphs acts
primitively on the set of edges, and thus provide infinitely many examples of
locally arc transitive edge transitive graphs with two orbits on vertices.
Finally, for each of these graphs we determine the full automorphism group,
together with the action on the set of vertices, of the subgroup that preserves
the edges.
  The study of locally arc transitive graphs with two orbits on vertices was
initiated by the first and third authors in [L. A. Duxbury and C. Praeger,
J. Algebraic Combin. 38 (2013), 407--429]. That paper contains a survey of the
results obtained up to that time, and outlines the main ideas of the approach
used here to construct the infinite families of locally arc transitive graphs
with the property that the automorphism group has two orbits on vertices and is
quasiprimitive on exactly one orbit, of twisted wreath type.
  The main idea in the construction of the graphs is to use a specific
construction of a twisted wreath graph, which was first introduced by Li in
[Qing X. Li, J. Algebraic Combin. 20 (2002), 147--164]. Li's construction
provides a natural way to obtain a locally arc transitive graph from a given
locally arc transitive graph and a group action on a set of vertices. The
success of the construction depends on the choice of the given locally arc
transitive graph and the group action. In this paper we show how to choose the
given graph and the group action so that the resulting graph is locally arc

recover a mixture of models for a sequence of categorical data. We show that

subject. We consider a quantum walker on a discrete, periodically driven
lattice. The walk is driven by an external source and coupled to a heat
reservoir. We derive an effective Floquet-Lindblad equation for the walker's
state and show that, under certain conditions, the system reaches a
non-equilibrium steady state. We analyze the steady state's properties and
show that the system exhibits non-thermal behavior. We also show that the
effective diffusion rate and the steady state's temperature can be controlled
by adjusting the driving period and the coupling to the reservoir. Our results
provide a fundamental understanding of periodically driven quantum walks and
may be used to design quantum devices that can be controlled in time.
Furthermore, we show that the model can be used to study the dynamics of
periodically driven quantum harmonic oscillators. We show that the effective
Floquet-Lindblad equation can be mapped to a time-dependent Caldeira-Leggett
model. We also show that the driven oscillator can be used to study the
dynamics of a quantum walker on a random lattice.

time-dependent Lindblad equation for open quantum systems that are periodically
driven. We show that the standard approach to derive a Lindblad equation is
incomplete and may lead to incorrect results. We also show that the method can
be used to derive a Floquet-Lindblad equation for quantum systems that are
coupled to a time-dependent reservoir.

the dynamics of a quantum repeater that is used to amplify weak quantum signals

detection algorithm that uses texture to improve edge quality. We train a
separate network to predict texture maps for the input image, and use the

chatbots, have become ubiquitous. However, these interfaces are limited to
understanding and generating human language in a narrow domain. They are not

learns to generate coherent and grammatically correct text by training a
language model on a large corpus of text and then fine-tuning it on dialog
transcripts. We evaluate our approach on two datasets: a popular dialog
dataset and a dataset of customer service transcripts. Our approach outperforms
state-of-the-art dialog generation models on these datasets.

information on the inhomogeneities velocity. We also show that the material
properties can be recovered from the time evolution of the bubble zone. We
propose a reconstruction algorithm based on the analysis of the time evolution
of the bubble zone. The proposed algorithm is able to recover the material
properties from a single measurement. The algorithm is tested on both
numerically simulated data and experimental data. The algorithm is able to
recover the material properties with high accuracy.

scans, called "Luminosity Jump
Scans" (LJS), have been implemented at the CERN Large Hadron Collider (LHC) in
2015 and 2016. These scans were performed by suddenly changing the beam
optics, in order to move the collision point across the transverse plane,
while keeping the bunch train frequency constant. The purpose of these scans
was to measure the luminosity-dependent systematic effects of the luminometers
and the bunch current monitors. The LJS scans were performed by suddenly
changing the beam optics, in order to move the collision point across the
transverse plane, while keeping the bunch train frequency constant. The
luminosity at the interaction point (IP) was varied by changing the horizontal
beam optics, by moving the upstream septum magnets. The LJS scans were
performed in several different configurations, by varying the horizontal and
vertical beam optics, and by changing the beam energy. The LJS scans have
provided a wealth of information on the luminosity-dependent systematic effects
of the luminometers and the BLMs, and have helped to improve the accuracy of
the luminosity measurement at the LHC.
  In this paper, the LJS scans performed in 2015 and 2016 are reviewed, and the
results are presented. The LJS scans have been used to measure the luminosity
dependent effects of the ALFA, CMS, ATLAS, and LHCb luminometers, and of the
BLMs installed in the LHC tunnel. The results have been used to improve the
luminosity measurement at the LHC, and to better understand the performance
and limitations of the LHC luminometers.
  The LJS scans have also been used to study the performance of the LHC
luminometers in different beam conditions, and to study the effects of the
luminosity-dependent effects on the luminosity measurement. The results have
been used to improve the LHC luminometers alignment and calibration, and to

communication networks focus on the average throughput of the networks. In
this paper, we take a step further to investigate the fairness of wireless
powered communication networks. We consider a downlink multi-user orthogonal
frequency division multiple (OFDM) based wireless powered communication system,
in which a wireless energy transmitter (WET) first broadcasts energy to a set of
single-antenna mobile devices (MDs) over the entire coverage area, and then a
base station (BS) assisted by the MDs transmit information to the MDs. The
fairness of the network is measured by the throughput each MD can achieve.
Under the constraint of the total energy available in the network, we aim to
design the optimal energy harvesting time, the transmit power of the BS, and
the data rate of each MD to maximize the network fairness. We formulate the
optimization problem as a non-linear programming problem, and solve it by
alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM). The proposed algorithm
achieves a near-optimal fairness performance with a low computational complexity
and is implementable in a distributed manner. Numerical results show that the
proposed algorithm can achieve a near-optimal fairness performance with a
reduced energy consumption.

devices (MDs) over the entire coverage area, and then a base station (BS) with
the assistance of the MDs transmit information to the MDs. The energy and
information transfer process is repeated for multiple times. The fairness of
the network is measured by the sum-throughput of the MDs. Under the constraint
of the total energy available in the network, we aim to design the optimal
energy harvesting time, the transmit power of the BS, and the data rate of each
MD to maximize the sum-throughput of the MDs. We formulate the optimization
problem as a mixed-integer non-linear programming problem, and solve it by
sequential convex programming (SCP). The proposed algorithm achieves a near
global optimal sum-throughput performance with a moderate computational
complexity. Numerical results show that the proposed algorithm can achieve a
near global optimal sum-throughput performance with a reduced energy consumption
and an improved network coverage.

performance of a CNN model trained on a small dataset. We also show that our
method can achieve comparable results to a model trained on a large dataset.

social networks. In this work, we propose a new method for community detection
based on the relative entropy optimization. The method is based on the
relaxation of the non-differentiable minimization problem with respect to the
membership matrix. The resulting optimization problem is solved efficiently
using the alternating direction method of multipliers. The performance of the
method is compared to the state-of-the-art methods on several social network
datasets.
  We show that the method outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in terms of
modularity and normalized mutual information. The method is also computationally
efficient, as it can process large social networks with millions of edges.
Moreover, the method is robust to the presence of outliers in the network, as
it is based on the relative entropy optimization, which is known to be
insensitive to outliers.

https://github.com/alexandrakuznetsov/RelEnt.

planetary system to another
through cometary impacts is an attractive mechanism for explaining the rapid
spread of life across Earth-like planets in a habitable galaxy. However, the
probability of life surviving the journey from one planetary system to another
is unknown. We investigate the survival of microorganisms during the passage
of a comet through the heliosphere and the subsequent atmospheric entry of a
comet nucleus. The heliospheric passage is dominated by the solar wind, which
causes a significant loss of microorganisms. The atmospheric entry is
dominated by friction, which causes a significant loss of microorganisms, but
the loss is reduced if the microorganisms are embedded in ice. The survival of
microorganisms during the passage of a comet through the heliosphere and the
atmosphere of a planet is dependent on the size of the comet, the size of the
microorganisms, the velocity of the comet, and the atmospheric properties of
the planet.
  We find that the survival of microorganisms during the heliospheric passage
is dominated by the size of the comet, with smaller comets being more
efficient at removing microorganisms. The survival of microorganisms during the
atmospheric entry is dominated by the size of the comet and the size of the
microorganisms, with smaller comets and smaller microorganisms being more
efficient at removing microorganisms. The atmospheric properties of the planet
also have a significant impact on the survival of microorganisms. The
atmospheric entry of a comet is more efficient at removing microorganisms if
the atmospheric density is high and the atmospheric temperature is low.
Microorganisms embedded in ice are more likely to survive the passage of a
comet through the heliosphere and the atmospheric entry of a comet nucleus.
Finally, we find that the survival of microorganisms during the passage of a
comet through the heliosphere and the atmospheric entry of a comet nucleus is
dependent on the velocity of the comet. The survival of microorganisms is
increased if the velocity of the comet is low.

other planets in the solar system. The results of this study are also relevant
to the search for life on exoplanets that are reached by comets. The results of
this study are also relevant to the search for life in the outer reaches of the
solar system, such as on Europa and Enceladus.

$G=(V,E)$ with edge costs $\{c_e:e\in E\}$. The goal is to find an edge set
$F\subseteq E$ that minimizes the total cost while satisfying some property
$\Pi$ of interest. In this work we consider the {\sc Min-Power $k$ Edge
Disjointness} problem, where $\Pi$ is the property of $F$ being $k$ edge
disjoint, i.e., $F$ cannot contain $k+1$ edge disjoint edges. We give a
$2^{\frac{1}{2}k+o(k)}$-approxiation algorithm for this problem, improving
upon the previously best known $2^k$-approximation algorithm of Chekuri and
Egambiyan (J. Algorithms 2018). Our result is obtained by using a new
relaxation of the $k$ edge disjointness constraint, which we call the
{\sc $k$-edge-disjoint-paths} relaxation. In this relaxation we allow $F$ to
contain sets of edges that are $k$ edge disjoint in the sense that there are
$k$ edge disjoint paths in $G$ that contain the edges of the set. We give a
$2^{\frac{1}{2}k+o(k)}$-approximation algorithm for the {\sc Min-Power
$K$-Edge-Disjoint-Paths} problem, where the goal is to find the minimum cost
edge set $F$ satisfying the $k$-edge-disjoint-paths constraint. We believe
that this relaxation is a promising approach for designing new algorithms
for minimum power network design problems.
  We also give a polynomial time algorithm for the special case where $G$ is a
tree. In this case we show that the optimal solution can be computed by
solving a system of linear equations. We believe that this result may be
useful for designing efficient algorithms for solving special cases of the
problem.
  All our results hold for arbitrary edge costs and for the objective of
minimizing the maximum edge cost. We believe that the {\sc Min-Power
$K$-Edge-Disjoint-Paths} problem is NP-hard for polynomially bounded costs,
unless $NP \subseteq P/poly$. We leave as an open question the determination of
the complexity of the problem for polynomially bounded costs.

study the localization of a quantum particle on a tree graph with a disordered
potential. We show that, in the localized phase, the wave function is
asymptotically described by a product of localized states at the nodes of the
graph. We derive an effective Hamiltonian for the asymptotic wave function and
show that, in the localized phase, the spectral gap in the effective
Hamiltonian is proportional to the connectivity of the graph. We also study the
distribution of the wave function in the localized phase and show that it is
described by a product of Fisher-Turquezie distributions. Our results are
relevant for the study of localization in graphs of arbitrary topology and
connectivity.

group flow of the tree graph model. We also show that the localization function
is related to the connectivity of the graph. Our results are relevant for the
study of localization in graphs of arbitrary topology and connectivity.

This methodology is based on a probabilistic model of the game that we
previously proposed. In this model, the outcome of a shot is determined by a

estimate the expected points that a defender will prevent a shooter from
scoring. We apply this methodology to data from the 2019-2020 NBA season and
analyze the expected points prevented by different defenders when facing
different shooters. We also analyze the expected points prevented by different
defenders when facing different shooting locations. We show that our model
captures the impact of the defender on the shooting process and we identify
specific defensive skills that some NBA players are better at than others.
Finally, we propose a new statistic to evaluate the effectiveness of a team's
defense. This statistic is based on the expected points prevented by a team
when facing a specific shooting location. We show that it is a better
differentiator of teams than the traditional defensive efficiency metric.

the form of a web application. This web application allows users to analyze
the defensive skills of NBA players and teams. It also allows users to
visualize the expected points prevented by a team when facing a specific

basketball fans and coaches. It will also be a platform to test our methodology

sequential data. However, RSSMs are typically trained using stochastic
backpropagation, which is computationally expensive and difficult to scale.
Furthermore, the learned parameters are not easily interpretable. In this work,
we propose a novel method for learning a deterministic RSSM that is easy to
interpret and computationally efficient to train. Our method, called
Deterministic Recurrent State-Space Model (DRSSM), uses a deterministic
activation function for the hidden states of the model and a novel
state-dependent noise model. We show that the resulting model is equivalent to
a nonlinear Gaussian state-space model with a recurrent observation equation.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of DRSSM on several sequential data analysis
tasks, including time-series forecasting and anomaly detection. We also show
that DRSSM can be used for interpretable modeling by learning a deterministic
RSSM that captures the underlying dynamics of a stochastic system.

triggered a renewed interest in understanding and controlling this phenomenon.
Here, we report on the observation of a large anomalous Nernst effect in
La$_{0.67}$Ca$_{0.33}$MnO$_3$ thin films. The anomalous Nernst coefficient is
found to be of the same order of magnitude as the anomalous Hall coefficient in
both temperature and magnetic field. We show that the anomalous Nernst effect
is a spin-dependent thermal transport process, which is controlled by the
magnetic field-induced skew scattering of electrons by magnetic moments. The
anomalous Nernst coefficient is found to be proportional to the spin-orbit
coupling and inversely proportional to the carrier density. Our results open
new perspectives for the investigation of spin-dependent thermal transport
phenomena in magnetic materials.

affects the academic performance of students with different personality traits.
Using a difference-in-difference-in-differences approach, we find that students
with a stronger work ethic tend to perform better under the remote learning
environment. In contrast, students with a higher level of extraversion tend to
perform worse. These results are obtained after controlling for individual
fixed effects, peer composition, and a wide range of covariates. Our findings
have important implications for how to mitigate the negative effects of the

problem. The algorithm is based on the idea of alternating minimization, where
in each iteration, we solve two least squares problems. The first problem is
solved along the factors, while the second problem is solved along the
corresponding elements of the data matrix. We show that the proposed algorithm
converges faster than the state-of-the-art algorithm, which is based on
conjugate gradient.

data points that are corrupted by outliers. The robust method is obtained by
applying the L1 norm penalty to the factorization problem. We show that the
robust method outperforms the state-of-the-art robust dimensionality reduction
method.

datasets, MNIST, and Caltech 101. The results are compared to the state-of-the-
art dimensionality reduction methods, including PCA, t-SNE, and UMAP. The

automorphism is completely determined by the set of roots it fixes.

direct product of $n$ copies of $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$. Moreover, such an
automorphism is completely determined by its action on the set of simple roots
and we will use a group theoretical argument to show that the group of such
automorphisms has a subgroup of index $n$.

$A_n$ hold also for the groups $B_n$, $C_n$ and $D_n$.

service have become popular
tools for organizations that want to leverage AI without investing in
infrastructure. However, these services also pose risks to the organizations
that use them. For example, a training service may leak sensitive information
about the data it is trained on, or a model service may return a model that
behaves in ways that are undesirable to the organization. We present a
framework for analyzing these risks, which we call the Risk Analysis
Framework for Machine Learning (RAF-ML). RAF-ML provides a structured way of
identifying and analyzing risks associated with outsourced machine learning,
enabling organizations to make informed decisions about how to mitigate those
risks.
  We demonstrate the utility of RAF-ML by applying it to a real-world
organization, the New York City Police Department (NYPD). We identify risks in
the NYPD's use of machine learning, including the risk that the data used to
train facial recognition models will contain sensitive information about
individuals. We then demonstrate how the framework can be used to mitigate
these risks, including by using differential privacy to remove sensitive
information from the data. We also discuss the challenges of applying the
framework in practice, including the difficulty of obtaining information about
the risks associated with a particular machine learning system.
  In conclusion, we argue that RAF-ML is a useful tool for analyzing the risks
associated with outsourced machine learning. We hope that it will be adopted by
organizations that use machine learning, and that it will be extended and
refined by future work.
  We also release a companion dataset of 1,000 machine learning systems
extracted from the Kaggle platform. The dataset includes information about the
systems, including the type of data they are trained on, the algorithms used
to train them, and the companies that provide the services that train them.
Together, the framework and the dataset provide a rich resource for
investigating the risks associated with outsourced machine learning.
  Finally, we release a companion report that provides a detailed example of
how RAF-ML can be used to analyze the risks associated with a real-world
machine learning system. The report includes a step-by-step example of how to
apply the framework, and it provides a detailed discussion of the results
obtained.

dependence of the speed of light can be described by an effective potential in
which the energy acts as a source of gravity. This leads to a new

binary pulsars and the recent measurements of the speed of light in the
laboratory. The model is also tested by adopting the Einstein formula for the
surface gravity of a neutron star. The predictions of the model are in
agreement with the recent observations of the millisecond pulsar PSR J0740+6620.

from the surface of a neutron star or by high-precision measurements of the

networks. We consider a multi-agent network in which each agent has a local
dataset and wishes to learn a shared model. The agents communicate with each
other over a time-invariant directed graph. We propose a distributed
stochastic gradient descent (DSGD) algorithm that achieves the optimal
convergence rate of $O(1/k)$, where $k$ is the iteration number. Moreover, we

agent to transmit a constant number of bytes per iteration. Finally, we
implement our proposed algorithm in a real-world experiment using a network of
wireless sensor nodes. The experimental results show that our algorithm can
learn a shared model with a high accuracy while significantly reducing the

automated grading of programming assignments. These models have shown to

and questions for practical adoption. In this paper, we present a learning-to-
grade system that integrates several machine learning models to automate the
grading of programming assignments. We also present a set of experiments
designed to answer several questions that are relevant to practical adoption.

while also being robust to several sources of variation. We also present a
discussion of several challenges and future research directions.

develop and evaluate learning-to-grade systems. The dataset includes the
source code of the assignments, the correct output of each program, and the
scores assigned by two human graders. We also release a set of 20 programs
written in Java that can be used to evaluate the performance of learning-to-
grade systems. The programs are designed to test the ability of such systems
to handle a variety of programming concepts and techniques.
  In summary, this paper presents a learning-to-grade system, presents
experiments designed to answer questions relevant to practical adoption, and
releases a dataset and a set of programs for the benefit of the research

using a fast global illumination renderer. We train the network to predict
per-pixel albedo, normal, and ambient occlusion maps, and we use a novel
normal-prediction approach that is able to generate detailed, smooth, and

uses a novel precomputation step to reduce rendering time. We demonstrate that
our approach is able to generate photorealistic results with a significant
reduction in rendering time compared to traditional rendering methods.

which makes it more practical for real-world applications. We evaluate our
approach on a dataset of 100 objects and demonstrate that it outperforms
previous approaches in terms of visual quality and rendering time.

embeddings have become a
prime focus in recent years. These node embeddings have been used in various
applications such as node classification, anomaly detection, and link
prediction. However, most of the existing methods assume that the input graph
is undirected and unweighted. In this paper, we focus on the problem of
learning structural role-based node embeddings for directed and multitype
graphs. We propose a novel method called Directed Structural Role Embedding
(DSRE) to learn structural role-based node embeddings for directed and
multitype graphs. DSRE uses a bipartite graph representation to model the
asymmetric and multitype nature of the input graph. It uses a novel
formulation to compute the node embedding by aggregating the structural role
embeddings of the neighbors. We conduct extensive experiments on six real
world datasets to evaluate the performance of DSRE. Experimental results show
that DSRE performs significantly better than the baseline methods.
Experimental results also show that DSRE is scalable and can handle large
multitype directed graphs.

person Re-Identification~(ReID) named Dual-Path Contrastive Network~(DPCN).
DPCN is designed to solve the problem of cross-source UDA, which aims to
adapt a model trained on a source domain to a target domain. DPCN is composed
of two paths. The first path is a contrastive learning~(CL) path. The CL path
is trained to minimize the distance between the source domain~(SD) and the
target domain~(TD) by a CL loss. The second path is a domain-invariant path.
The domain-invariant path is trained to minimize the distance between the
training data distribution and the target data distribution by a domain
invariant loss. We validate the effectiveness of DPCN on three cross-source
UDA datasets. The results show that DPCN achieves state-of-the-art performance
and outperforms the state-of-the-art methods by a large margin.

important in a wide variety of environments, including in dark matter halos
with virial temperatures $T_{\rm vir}\gtrsim 3000$ K.

electricity market design. This paper investigates the impact of day-ahead
market design on the integration of variable renewable energy sources. We
simulate different market designs under high shares of wind power in Germany
using the open-source power market simulator PyPSA. We find that a locational
margin pricing (LMP) scheme is superior to uniform pricing in terms of
revenue adequacy, price volatility, and efficiency. LMP leads to higher
revenue for generators and consumers, lower price volatility, and lower
inefficiencies compared to uniform pricing. LMP is also more flexible in
adjusting for changes in load and generation. We find that a bidding zone
structure is not necessary for LMP to be effective. However, a bidding zone
structure can be used to further reduce price volatility and increase revenue
adequacy. We find that a bidding zone structure is more important than the
size of the bidding zones themselves.
  We also investigate the impact of forward contracts on the integration of
wind power. We find that forward contracts can lead to price volatility in the
day-ahead market and reduce efficiency. Forward contracts can also lead to
inefficiencies in the balancing market. We find that forward contracts are
more important than the size of the forward market itself.
  We conclude that locational margin pricing is a suitable market design for
high shares of wind power. However, further research is needed to investigate
the impact of forward contracts and bidding zones in more detail.
  We provide a Python package for power market simulation that can be used to
investigate the impact of different market designs. The package is available
online at https://github.com/pschuller/pypsasim.

margin pricing, forward contracts, bidding zones, power market simulation
software

(MSSM) in the case where the Higgs sector does not participate in the breaking
of family symmetries. We consider the most general superpotential compatible
with the family symmetries and we assume that the Higgs fields do not couple
to the family lepton superfields. We study the spectrum of superparticles and
the production of supersymmetric particles at the LHC. We find that the
non-renormalizable interactions in the superpotential have a significant
impact on the spectrum of superparticles and on the production of supersymmetric
particles at the LHC. We also find that the experimental limits on the
parameter space of the model are still to be fully explored. Finally, we
demonstrate that the future LHC run will be able to probe the parameter space
of the model and possibly discover supersymmetric particles.

most intense auroral activity in the
Solar System. The main driver of this activity is the interaction between
Saturn's magnetosphere and the solar wind. The solar wind is expected to
accelerate electrons and ions in Saturn's polar magnetosphere. The resulting
current system is expected to be closed by a field-aligned current (FAC) in the
polar ionosphere. The FAC is driven by the imbalance of the momentum transfer
between the solar wind and the magnetosphere. The resulting ionospheric currents
are expected to drive the auroral activity. However, the detailed processes
between the solar wind and the auroral activity are still unknown. In this
paper, we present a new model of the auroral activity at Saturn, which is
developed based on the interaction between the solar wind and the magnetosphere
of Saturn. The model is developed to investigate the relationship between the
solar wind and the auroral activity at Saturn. The model is composed of three
sub-models. The first sub-model is the solar wind-magnetosphere coupling
model, which is used to calculate the FAC in the polar magnetosphere. The
FAC-driven ionospheric currents are calculated by the second sub-model. The
final sub-model is the ionospheric auroral model, which is used to calculate the
auroral brightness based on the ionospheric currents. The model is applied to
the solar wind conditions of March 20, 2013. The results show that the
magnetospheric interaction with the solar wind is the main driver of the
auroral activity at Saturn. The model is useful for investigating the
relationship between the solar wind and the auroral activity at Saturn.
Furthermore, the model can be used to investigate the effects of solar wind
variations on the auroral activity at Saturn.

furthermore show that the presence of dissipation leads to a loss of

describes the time evolution of the condensate Wigner function. We show that

coherence. We further show that the SLE can be simplified to a set of coupled
GPGPEs that describe the evolution of the momentum sidebands of the condensate.

condensate in the presence of dissipation.

the Quantum Theory of Gravity led several authors to consider new approaches
based on radically different foundations. Among these, Causal Set Theory
stands out for its simplicity and beauty. Unfortunately, due to its technical

disadvantages of this approach to Quantum Gravity.

predicts a relation between two or more entities in the text, rather than

  We also present a new method for training relational prediction models,
which we call {\it relational distillation}. In relational distillation, a
model is trained to predict a relation by being trained on a set of examples
with the same relation. We show that relational distillation achieves higher
accuracy than traditional training on the new discourse marker dataset, and
also on a standard English semantic role labeling dataset.

from the use of contextualized embeddings, such as BERT. We show that models
trained using BERT achieve higher accuracy than models trained using GloVe,

semidefinite (PSD) matrix variable and a term involving the Cholesky (or
symmetric matrix square root) of a function of the variable. Such a problem
arises in the context of matrix nearness problems, matrix polynomial
optimization, and matrix factorization. We show that the objective function
is geodesically convex on the symmetric positive definite matrices, and thus
minimized on the unit simplex of PSD matrices. Moreover, we show that the
geodesic convexity is sufficient to compute the optimal value and the
corresponding optimal symmetric matrix square root using first-order methods.
  We also study the case when the rank of the variable is fixed. In this case
the optimal solution is attained at a rank-one matrix. We show that the
objective function is geodesically strictly convex on the rank-one positive
semidefinite matrices, and thus has a unique global minimum. Moreover, we show
that the optimal value and the corresponding optimal symmetric matrix square
root can be computed using first-order methods. Finally, we study a special
case of rank-one optimization where the square root of a function of the
variable is replaced by the logarithm of the function of the variable. We show
that the resulting problem is geodesically strictly convex and can be solved
using first-order methods.

grossing, netting, novating, and collateral netting. We also discuss the
different types of collateral that can be used in netting, including cash,
securities, and derivatives. We provide an overview of the rules and
regulations that govern netting, including the 2006 ISDA Collateral Agreement,
the 2013 ISDA Mutual Collateral Agreement, the 2015 ISDA Variation Margin
Agreement, and the 2016 EU Central Counterparty (CCP) Regulation. We also
discuss the various clearinghouses and CCPs that use netting, including LCH
Clearing, CME Clearing, and the Depository Trust and Clearing Corporation
(DTCC).
  We also discuss the challenges and future directions of netting. We provide
an overview of the current risks and issues associated with netting, including
the risk of counterparty default, the risk of insolvency, and the risk of
regulatory change. We also discuss the future directions of netting, including
the use of distributed ledger technology, the use of artificial intelligence,
and the use of machine learning.
  In conclusion, netting is a complex and multifaceted concept that is
central to the functioning of financial markets. It is essential that
researchers and practitioners in the field of netting have a comprehensive

multiple language pairs for multilingual semantic space construction. In
contrast to the existing approaches that use the parallel corpora in a single

simultaneously constructs multiple parallel semantic spaces from the parallel

then integrated into a common multilingual semantic space. We evaluate the
proposed approach on English-German and English-French language pairs. The

illustrated by simulating a nonlinear system with a safety constraint. The

  Methods. We use the 2016-2018 Medical Expenditure Panel Survey (MEPS) to
analyze the impact of SDoH on healthcare costs and utilization. We use a
multivariate regression model to control for individual and household
characteristics. We also use a propensity score matching (PSM) method to
control for the selection bias. We estimate the average treatment effect on
the treated (ATTT) to quantify the impact of SDoH on healthcare costs and
utilization.
  Results. We find that SDoH have a significant impact on healthcare costs and
utilization. Individuals with SDoH are more likely to have higher healthcare
costs and utilization. The ATTT estimates indicate that individuals with SDoH
have $1,500 to $2,000 higher annual healthcare costs compared to those without
SDoH. The ATTT estimates also indicate that individuals with SDoH have 1.5 to 2
more outpatient visits and 1.2 to 1.5 more inpatient stays compared to those
without SDoH.
  Conclusion. Our study provides evidence that SDoH have a significant impact on
healthcare costs and utilization. The findings of this study can be used to
develop targeted interventions to mitigate the impact of SDoH on healthcare
costs and utilization.
  Limitations. The MEPS data does not have information on the severity of SDoH
and the duration of SDoH. Future studies can use administrative claims data
and longitudinal studies to investigate the impact of SDoH on healthcare costs

Variables (CVs) with the strongest
magnetic fields, known as Synchronous Polarized Systems (SPOLs), are of great
interest for the study of accretion and magnetism in CVs. The only known
spectropolarimetric study of SPOLs was performed in 2000, and since then, the
field has grown significantly. We present new spectropolarimetric observations
of the SPOLs AE Leo and TV Col, taken in 2019 with the SMARTS 1.5m telescope
and the CHIRON spectrograph. We also present a re-analysis of the data from
2000. We find that the polarized emission of both sources is consistent with
being produced in a white dwarf (WD) magnetosphere. We also find that the
magnetic field of AE Leo is stronger than previously reported, and that the
spin period of TV Col is shorter than previously reported. We find that the
spin period of TV Col is consistent with being synchronized with its orbital
period, and that AE Leo is in a state of spin-up. We also find that the
accretion rate of TV Col is higher than previously reported, and that the
accretion rate of AE Leo is consistent with being in the range of typical
non-magnetic CVs. We discuss the implications of our findings for the
classification of these sources, and the role of magnetic fields in the
accretion process.

object-oriented and functional type systems. The type system is realized in
Haskell, a functional programming language that supports type systems. In
Haskell, we define a type constructor for defining object-oriented types and
implement a type checker that checks the type system. We demonstrate the
approach by defining a simple banking system that combines object-oriented and
functional programming.
